original: Волков бояться — в лес не ходить.
transliteration: Volkov boyat'sya — v les ne khodit'.
translation: If you're afraid of wolves, don't go into the forest.
meaning: If you fear every risk, you'll never do anything worthwhile.
note: Said to someone hesitating over a risky step. The wolves stand in for whatever danger you have to accept to get what the forest offers: firewood, mushrooms, game.

translation: The slower you ride, the farther you'll get.
meaning: Rushing wears you out; a steady pace gets you further in the end.
equivalent: Slow and steady wins the race.
note: An old coaching proverb: horses driven hard early won't last the journey. Тише here means "slower", not "quieter".

original: Без труда не вытащишь и рыбку из пруда.
transliteration: Bez truda ne vytashchish' i rybku iz pruda.
translation: Without effort, you can't even pull a little fish out of a pond.
meaning: Nothing comes without work, not even the easy things.
note: One of the first proverbs Russian children learn. Рыбка is the diminutive "little fish": even the smallest prize takes work.

original: Не имей сто рублей, а имей сто друзей.
transliteration: Ne imey sto rubley, a imey sto druzey.
translation: Don't have a hundred rubles — have a hundred friends.
meaning: Friendships are worth more than money.
note: The rhyme of рублей and друзей makes it stick. It's a staple of toasts and birthday cards.

translation: The morning is wiser than the evening.
meaning: Don't make decisions when you're tired; a rested mind sees more clearly.
note: Familiar from Russian fairy tales, where a helper tells the troubled hero to go to sleep. By morning, the impossible task has been solved.

original: Не в свои сани не садись.
transliteration: Ne v svoi sani ne sadis'.
translation: Don't climb into a sleigh that isn't yours.
meaning: Don't take on roles or ambitions that don't suit you.
note: Also the title of an 1853 comedy by Alexander Ostrovsky, about a merchant's daughter who runs off with a nobleman.

translation: Moscow wasn't built all at once.
meaning: Great things take time.
equivalent: Rome wasn't built in a day.
note: The Russian counterpart of the Roman proverb, with the city that mattered at home swapped in.

translation: Fall down seven times, get up eight.
meaning: However many times you fail, get back up.
equivalent: If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
note: The extra "eight" is the point: you always rise once more than you fall. The daruma doll, weighted to pop back upright, is its emblem.

translation: Even monkeys fall from trees.
meaning: Even experts make mistakes.
note: Said kindly when a skilled person slips up — a way of saying the mistake doesn't define them.

translation: Dumplings rather than flowers.
meaning: Practical benefits matter more than beauty.
note: Born from hanami, the cherry-blossom picnic, where many guests care more about the food than the blossoms. Often used teasingly.

translation: The stake that sticks out gets hammered down.
meaning: Whoever stands out attracts criticism.
equivalent: The tall poppy gets cut down.
note: Often cited as a comment on conformity in Japan — and just as often quoted by people who stick out anyway.

original: 井の中の蛙大海を知らず
transliteration: i no naka no kawazu taikai o shirazu
translation: A frog in a well knows nothing of the great ocean.
meaning: Narrow experience gives a narrow view of the world.
note: Borrowed from the Chinese classic Zhuangzi. Japanese later added a hopeful ending: されど空の青さを知る, "but it knows the blueness of the sky."

transliteration: ishi no ue ni mo sannen
translation: Even on a stone — three years.
meaning: Persevere, and even hardship eventually gives way.
note: Sit on a cold stone for three years and it will grow warm. It is often offered to new employees who want to quit early.

translation: One time, one meeting.
meaning: Every encounter happens only once, so treasure it.
note: Rooted in the tea ceremony. The host prepares each gathering as if it can never be repeated — because, exactly as it is, it can't.

transliteration: Qiān lǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià.
translation: A journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet.
meaning: Great undertakings start with a single small action.
equivalent: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
note: A li is a traditional unit of distance, about half a kilometre. The familiar English version comes from this line, which literally speaks of the ground under your feet rather than a step.

transliteration: Sài wēng shī mǎ, yān zhī fēi fú.
translation: The old man at the frontier lost his horse — who's to say it wasn't a blessing?
meaning: In the moment, good and bad fortune are hard to tell apart.
note: The horse runs off, then returns with a fine stallion. The son breaks his leg riding it, and the injury keeps him out of a war that kills most young men. At every turn, the old man refuses to call it good or bad.

transliteration: Sān rén xíng, bì yǒu wǒ shī.
translation: When three people walk together, one of them can surely be my teacher.
meaning: You can learn something from anyone.
note: Confucius continues: follow their good qualities, and use their bad ones to correct yourself.

translation: Drawing a snake and adding feet.
meaning: Ruining something by overdoing it.
note: In a race to draw a snake for a jug of wine, the fastest artist had time to spare, so he added feet — and lost, because snakes don't have feet.

translation: Playing the qin to a cow.
meaning: Wasting refined words on an audience that can't appreciate them.
note: The qin is the seven-string zither of scholars. The phrase can scold the listener for not getting it — or the speaker for choosing the wrong audience.

translation: Mending the pen after a sheep is lost.
meaning: Fix a problem even after a loss, before it gets worse.
note: The original line goes on: 未为迟也, "it is not too late." Compare the Korean proverb about fixing the barn after the cow is gone, which draws the opposite lesson.

translation: Guarding a tree stump, waiting for rabbits.
meaning: Waiting for luck to strike twice instead of working.
note: A farmer saw a rabbit run into a stump and break its neck. He abandoned his plough to wait for another; his fields went to ruin and he became a laughingstock.

original: 가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다
transliteration: ganeun mari gowaya oneun mari gopda
translation: Only if the words going out are kind will the words coming back be kind.
meaning: Treat others the way you want to be treated.
note: A gentle reminder that the tone of a conversation is set by whoever speaks first.

original: 낮말은 새가 듣고 밤말은 쥐가 듣는다
transliteration: nanmareun saega deutgo bammareun jwiga deunneunda
translation: Birds hear the words of the day; mice hear the words of the night.
meaning: Someone is always listening, so be careful what you say.
note: Revised Romanization follows pronunciation, which is why 낮말 becomes "nanmal" rather than "natmal".

translation: Even a tiger comes when you talk about it.
meaning: The person you're talking about often shows up.
note: Tigers once roamed the Korean peninsula and fill its folklore, where they are as often foolish as fearsome.

translation: Even a sheet of paper is better lifted together.
meaning: Cooperation helps, even with small tasks.
note: The point is that no job is too small to share.

translation: Fixing the barn after losing the cow.
meaning: Taking precautions only after it's too late.
equivalent: Closing the barn door after the horse has bolted.
note: Where the Chinese idiom 亡羊补牢 says it's never too late to mend the pen, the Korean version mocks the fix as pointless. Same image, opposite moral.

translation: Eating rice cake lying down.
meaning: Something extremely easy.
note: Tteok is chewy rice cake. Its English cousin also reaches for cake — though eating tteok lying down would actually be quite hard.

translation: Gather specks of dust and you get Mount Tai.
meaning: Small amounts add up.
note: Mount Tai in China was the classic image of something vast. The saying is a favourite of savers — and of bank adverts.

translation: Patience is the key to relief.
meaning: Endure hard times patiently and relief will come.
equivalent: Good things come to those who wait.
note: Faraj means release from hardship. The saying is used to comfort someone waiting out a difficult time.

translation: Whoever strives, finds.
meaning: Effort is rewarded.
equivalent: Where there's a will, there's a way.
note: Two short verbs that almost mirror each other. It's a favourite of schoolteachers and is often written on classroom walls.

translation: The neighbour before the house.
meaning: Choose your neighbours before you choose your home.
note: Neighbourliness carries great weight in Arab tradition. A fine house next to bad neighbours is no bargain.

translation: What's past is dead.
meaning: Leave old grievances behind.
note: Colloquial rather than classical Arabic, heard across Egypt and the Levant. The rhyme of fāt and māt gives it snap.

translation: Every vessel seeps what it holds.
meaning: People reveal their true nature through what they say and do.
note: Often quoted after someone says something unkind: the words say more about the speaker than the target.

translation: Every occasion has its fitting words.
meaning: Match what you say to the situation.
equivalent: There's a time and a place for everything.
note: A principle of classical Arabic rhetoric (balāgha): true eloquence means fitting the speech to the moment.

translation: The eye doesn't rise above the eyebrow.
meaning: Respect those above you — elders, superiors, tradition.
note: Said to someone who oversteps with an elder or a boss. Colloquial versions differ from dialect to dialect.

translation: This too is for the good.
meaning: Even setbacks may turn out for the best.
note: The Talmud links it to Nahum Ish Gamzu, who said it whatever befell him. The pun on his name, Gamzu, is part of the story.

original: אם אין אני לי, מי לי?
transliteration: im ein ani li, mi li?
translation: If I am not for myself, who will be for me?
meaning: Take responsibility for yourself — but not only for yourself.
note: Hillel goes on: "And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?" The three lines balance self-reliance, generosity and urgency.

translation: There is nothing new under the sun.
meaning: Whatever is happening has happened before.
note: English borrowed the phrase directly through the King James Bible. In both languages it's used wearily and wryly.

translation: All beginnings are hard.
meaning: The start is the hardest part; don't be discouraged by it.
note: Rooted in rabbinic commentary, it's now everyday Israeli encouragement for anyone starting something new. German has the same saying: Aller Anfang ist schwer.

translation: Grasp too much, and you've grasped nothing.
meaning: Overreaching leaves you with nothing.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew.
note: Originally a Talmudic legal principle: when in doubt, take the smaller amount, because it's certain. Now used for any overambitious plan.

original: אל תסתכל בקנקן, אלא במה שיש בו
transliteration: al tistakel ba-kankan, ela ba-meh she-yesh bo
translation: Don't look at the jug, but at what's inside it.
meaning: Judge people by their substance, not their appearance.
equivalent: Don't judge a book by its cover.
note: Rabbi Meir continues: "There is a new jug full of old wine, and an old jug without even new wine in it."

translation: As you act, so you will pay.
meaning: Your actions come back to you.
note: A folk echo of the idea of karma. The rhyming pair karnī (doing) and bharnī (paying back) makes it easy to remember.

translation: A half-filled pot keeps splashing over.
meaning: Those with a little knowledge make the most show of it.
equivalent: Empty vessels make the most noise.
note: A full pot, carried carefully, doesn't spill. The verb forms come from older Hindi dialects, which gives it a rustic, timeless ring.

original: अब पछताए होत क्या, जब चिड़िया चुग गई खेत
transliteration: ab pachhtāe hot kyā, jab chiṛiyā chug gaī khet
translation: What use is regret now, when the birds have already picked the field clean?
meaning: Regret is pointless once the damage is done.
equivalent: No use crying over spilt milk.
note: A farmer who didn't guard his crop has only himself to blame. The first half is in an older, poetic register.

translation: A chicken at home is worth no more than lentils.
meaning: We undervalue what we already have.
note: Chicken is a treat and dal an everyday staple — but the chicken you raise yourself stops feeling special.

translation: Can't dance, so blames the crooked courtyard.
meaning: Blaming circumstances for your own lack of skill.
equivalent: A bad workman blames his tools.
note: The āṅgan is the open courtyard at the heart of a traditional house, where celebrations and dancing take place.

original: बंदर क्या जाने अदरक का स्वाद
transliteration: bandar kyā jāne adrak kā svād
translation: What does a monkey know of the taste of ginger?
meaning: Some people can't appreciate something fine.
note: A common playful insult, the kind traded between friends.

original: जल में रहकर मगर से बैर
transliteration: jal meṁ rahkar magar se bair
translation: Living in the water, yet feuding with the crocodile.
meaning: Don't make enemies of the powerful people you live alongside.
note: A warning to anyone — an employee, a tenant — tempted to pick a fight with whoever controls their surroundings.

original: از تو حرکت، از خدا برکت
transliteration: az to harekat, az khodā barekat
translation: From you, the effort; from God, the blessing.
meaning: Do your part and good fortune will follow.
equivalent: God helps those who help themselves.
note: The rhyme of harekat and barekat carries it. Iranians use it to nudge someone into getting started.

translation: Accounts are accounts, and a brother is a brother.
meaning: Keep money matters straight, even with family.
note: Kākā is an affectionate, old-fashioned word for brother. Love your family — but keep the books.

original: تا تنور گرم است باید نان را چسباند
transliteration: tā tanur garm ast, bāyad nān rā chasbānd
translation: While the oven is hot, slap the bread on.
meaning: Act while the opportunity lasts.
equivalent: Strike while the iron is hot.
note: Flatbreads like lavash are slapped against the inside wall of a clay tanur oven. Wait too long and it cools.

original: هر که بامش بیش، برفش بیشتر
transliteration: har ke bāmash bish, barfash bishtar
translation: The bigger your roof, the more snow falls on it.
meaning: More wealth or status brings more burdens.
equivalent: Heavy is the head that wears the crown.
note: Flat roofs had to be cleared by hand after snowfall — a chore that grew with the size of the house.

translation: The Shahnameh has a happy ending.
meaning: Don't celebrate too early; things may yet end badly.
equivalent: It ain't over till it's over.
note: Ferdowsi's epic Book of Kings actually ends in tragedy, with the fall of the Sasanian empire. The irony is the point.

original: مارگزیده از ریسمان سیاه و سفید می‌ترسد
transliteration: mār-gazide az rismān-e siyāh o sefid mitarsad
translation: Someone bitten by a snake fears a black-and-white rope.
meaning: A bad experience makes you wary of anything that resembles it.
note: The striped rope looks just enough like a snake to make the once-bitten jump.

original: کوه به کوه نمی‌رسد، آدم به آدم می‌رسد
transliteration: kuh be kuh nemiresad, ādam be ādam miresad
translation: Mountains never meet, but people do.
meaning: You'll cross paths with people again, so treat them well.
note: Said warmly at a parting — or as a quiet warning to someone who has behaved badly.

translation: Drop by drop, a lake forms.
meaning: Small amounts add up over time.
note: Close cousins appear across cultures — compare the Swahili haba na haba and the Korean dust that becomes a mountain.

translation: Keep the straw — its time will come.
meaning: Don't throw things away; you may need them later.
note: Straw seems worthless until winter fodder runs short. The rhyme of samanı and zamanı keeps it memorable.

original: Bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır.
translation: A single cup of coffee is remembered for forty years.
meaning: Even a small kindness creates a lasting bond.
note: Turkish coffee is a gesture of hospitality, and forty is a traditional number for "a very long time".

translation: A tree is bent while it's young.
meaning: Habits and character are shaped early.
equivalent: As the twig is bent, so grows the tree.
note: Yaş means both "age" and "green, fresh" — a green sapling bends, a dry old trunk breaks.

translation: The patient dervish attained his wish.
meaning: Patience is rewarded.
equivalent: Good things come to those who wait.
note: Dervishes, the Sufi mystics, were models of patience. The -miş ending is the storytelling past tense, so it sounds like the end of a tale.

translation: A grape darkens by looking at another grape.
meaning: People take on the habits of those around them.
equivalent: You are the company you keep.
note: Grapes on a bunch ripen together, as if they were copying each other.

translation: A friend speaks bitter words.
meaning: A true friend tells you the hard truth.
note: Flatterers say what you want to hear; a real friend says what you need to hear.

original: En boca cerrada no entran moscas.
translation: Flies don't get into a closed mouth.
meaning: Keeping quiet keeps you out of trouble.
note: Advice for moments when saying anything at all can only make things worse.

original: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.
translation: The shrimp that falls asleep gets swept away by the current.
meaning: If you're not alert, you'll miss out or be left behind.
note: Especially popular in Latin America, often shortened to just "camarón que se duerme…"

original: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
translation: There's no misfortune that doesn't bring some good.
meaning: Something good comes out of every bad situation.
equivalent: Every cloud has a silver lining.
note: Said to console someone after a setback — often with a knowing smile.

original: A caballo regalado no se le mira el diente.
translation: You don't check the teeth of a horse you were given.
meaning: Don't be critical of a gift.
equivalent: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
note: A horse's age is read from its teeth. The saying goes back at least to St Jerome, writing in Latin around 400 CE.

original: Más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo.
translation: The devil knows more from being old than from being the devil.
meaning: Experience teaches more than cleverness.
note: A favourite reply of grandparents when the young think they know better.

original: Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho.
translation: From saying to doing is a long stretch.
meaning: Promises are easy; following through is hard.
note: The triple rhyme — dicho, hecho, trecho — is what makes it quotable.

original: Cría cuervos y te sacarán los ojos.
translation: Raise crows and they'll peck your eyes out.
meaning: Those you help may turn against you.
equivalent: Bite the hand that feeds you.
note: It gave its name to Carlos Saura's 1976 film Cría cuervos.

translation: Whoever rests, rusts.
meaning: Stay active or you'll lose your abilities.
note: A favourite motto of German hiking clubs and fitness-minded retirees.

translation: Practice makes the master.
meaning: Skill comes from practice.
note: Meister is also a formal title in German crafts: a master craftsman who has passed the Meisterprüfung.

translation: End good, all good.
meaning: A good outcome makes up for the troubles along the way.
note: Short enough to say with a sigh of relief. It's also the German title of Shakespeare's play.

original: Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen.
translation: Whoever says A must also say B.
meaning: Once you've started something, you have to see it through.
equivalent: In for a penny, in for a pound.
note: Bertolt Brecht answered it in his play Der Jasager und der Neinsager: whoever says A doesn't have to say B, if they realize A was wrong.

translation: That's where the dog is buried.
meaning: That's the heart of the matter.
note: Its origin is disputed, with theories ranging from buried treasure to real dog graves. Nobody knows where the dog is buried.

translation: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
meaning: Those who start early get more done.
equivalent: The early bird catches the worm.
note: Often traced to the Latin Aurora musis amica, "dawn is a friend to the Muses."

translation: I only understand "train station".
meaning: I have no idea what you're talking about.
note: Often traced to soldiers at the end of the First World War, who could think of nothing but the station that would take them home.

translation: Know thyself.
meaning: Understand your own nature and limits.
note: One of the maxims inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi. Socrates made it central to philosophy.

translation: Nothing in excess.
meaning: Moderation in all things.
note: Also inscribed at Delphi, beside "know thyself". Moderation runs through Greek ethics, all the way to Aristotle's golden mean.

translation: Everything flows.
meaning: Nothing stays the same; change is constant.
note: Associated with Heraclitus, though these exact words come from later writers summarising him. His better-attested image: you can't step into the same river twice.

translation: One swallow does not make a spring.
meaning: One good sign doesn't mean a lasting change.
equivalent: One swallow doesn't make a summer.
note: Aristotle adds that one day, or a short time, doesn't make a person happy either. In English, the swallow moved to summer.

original: Η γλώσσα κόκαλα δεν έχει, αλλά κόκαλα τσακίζει.
transliteration: I glóssa kókala den échei, allá kókala tsakízei.
translation: The tongue has no bones, but it breaks bones.
meaning: Words can do real harm.
note: A popular modern Greek proverb, usually said as a warning before someone speaks in anger.

translation: Whoever hurries, stumbles.
meaning: Rushing leads to mistakes.
note: The ancient Greeks had their own version, σπεῦδε βραδέως — "hasten slowly" — which the Romans took up as festina lente.

translation: Every obstacle is for the good.
meaning: A setback may turn out to be lucky.
note: Said when plans fall through. Compare the Hebrew gam zo le-tova, "this too is for the good."

translation: Little by little fills the measure.
meaning: Small efforts add up.
note: A kibaba is a small traditional measure for grain. Perhaps the best-known Swahili proverb, it's often printed on kanga cloths.

translation: Slowly, slowly is the way to go.
meaning: A steady pace gets you there.
equivalent: Slow and steady wins the race.
note: Pole pole is heard constantly in East Africa. Every climber on Kilimanjaro hears it from their guides.

translation: Whoever doesn't listen to their elders breaks a leg.
meaning: Ignore wise advice at your peril.
note: Guu is a playful form of mguu (leg), chosen for the rhyme. It's a standard warning to headstrong children.

translation: Guest, come — so the host may prosper.
meaning: Guests bring blessings to the household.
note: When a visitor arrives, a better meal gets cooked, and the host eats well too. A warm way to welcome someone.

translation: One finger can't crush a louse.
meaning: Some things can only be done together.
note: An earthy image of cooperation: you need at least two fingers for even the smallest job.

translation: If you don't fill the crack, you'll be building a wall.
meaning: Fix small problems before they become big ones.
equivalent: A stitch in time saves nine.
note: Common in East African politics and journalism as a warning against ignoring early signs of trouble.

translation: Once water is spilled, it can't be gathered up.
meaning: Some things can't be undone.
equivalent: No use crying over spilt milk.
note: Sometimes used as a warning before acting rashly, not only as comfort afterwards.

translation: Character is beauty.
meaning: Good character matters more than good looks.
note: Ìwà (character) is central to Yoruba ethics. The ideal person, the ọmọlúàbí, is admired for conduct rather than appearance.

original: Igi kan kì í dágbó ṣe.
translation: One tree does not make a forest.
meaning: Strength comes from community, not individuals alone.
note: A reminder that no one achieves anything truly great alone.

translation: No single road leads into the market.
meaning: There is always more than one way to reach a goal.
equivalent: There's more than one way to skin a cat.
note: Yoruba markets drew traders along many paths — a reminder not to give up when one route is blocked.

translation: Home is where one returns to rest from the farm.
meaning: However far you go, home is where you find rest.
note: Often quoted to people living abroad, as a reminder that home is waiting.

original: Àgbà kì í wà lọ́jà kí orí ọmọ tuntun wọ́.
translation: Elders are not in the market and let a baby's head hang crooked.
meaning: Responsible people step in when something is wrong.
note: Babies are carried on their mothers' backs. An elder who sees a baby's head lolling is expected to fix it — it's a call to take responsibility.

original: Oma maa mansikka, muu maa mustikka.
translation: Your own land is a strawberry, other lands a blueberry.
meaning: Home is sweetest.
note: Both berries grow wild all over Finland — but the strawberry is the sweeter prize.

translation: No smoke without fire.
meaning: Rumours usually have some truth behind them.
note: Found in almost the same words across Europe. In Finland, land of saunas, smoke is rarely far away.

original: Joka kuuseen kurkottaa, se katajaan kapsahtaa.
translation: Whoever reaches for the spruce falls into the juniper.
meaning: Overreaching leads to a fall.
note: The alliteration of kuuseen kurkottaa and katajaan kapsahtaa is classic Finnish. Juniper is low and prickly — a painful place to land.

translation: Learning won't tip you into a ditch.
meaning: Knowledge is never wasted.
note: A reflection of Finland's deep respect for education.

original: Niin metsä vastaa kuin sinne huudetaan.
translation: The forest answers the way you shout into it.
meaning: How you treat others is how they'll treat you.
note: An echo in a forest returns exactly what you sent — kindness or rudeness alike.

translation: Diligence overcomes hard luck.
meaning: Hard work beats bad luck.
note: A plain-spoken favourite in a country with long winters and thin soil, where persistence was everything.

translation: No one is born a smith.
meaning: Every skill has to be learned.
note: The smith is a mythic figure in Finland — Ilmarinen forges the magical Sampo in the Kalevala — yet even smiths have to learn.
